Liposarcoma
Overview
Composed of various histologic forms related to the developmental stages of lipoblasts
Retroperitoneal lesions are more locally aggressive and more likely to dedifferentiate than
extremity lesions.
Well-differentiated liposarcomas and atypical lipomatous tumors can transform into a
dedifferentiated liposarcoma (also MDM2 positive). Rapid growth of a long-standing (usually >5
years), painless mass is suspicious.
Epidemiology

Second most common soft-tissue sarcoma in adults after undifferentiated pleomorphic
sarcoma (UPS)
Most common in individuals aged 50 to 80 years. Myxoid liposarcoma can occur in younger
adults.
Subtypes
Atypical lipomatous tumor/well-differentiated liposarcoma
Histologically, these entities are identical. The former term is for an extremity lesion, the
latter term is for a retroperitoneal location
Myxoid/round cell liposarcoma
Younger patient population (aged 30 to 60 years)
Translocation: t(12.16)(q13; p11)
Although the lungs remain the most common site, it is known to metastasize to
unconventional, nonpulmonary sites. Staging and surveillance imaging studies should
reflect these patterns.
Considered more sensitive to chemotherapy and radiation therapy.
Greater round cell component begets high grade and portends poorer prognosis.
Pleomorphic liposarcoma
Rare (≤5% of liposarcomas)
Age older than 60 years
May portend poorer diagnosis
P53 mutation; otherwise, no distinctive immunohistochemistry or chromosomal findings.
Dedifferentiated liposarcoma
Rare (<10% of cases); transformation into high-grade lesion in background setting of atypical
lipomatous tumor/well-differentiated liposarcoma.
MDM2 positive
Etiology
Liposarcoma originates from primitive mesenchymal cells; diagnosis does not require adipose
cells.
Simple lipomas do not predispose a patient to liposarcoma.
Well-differentiated variants have giant marker and ring chromosomes and overexpression of
MDM2 (Table 1).

Radiography
Plain radiographs occasionally demonstrate foci of calcification or ossification in well-

Computed Tomography
Myxoid liposarcomas can metastasize to sites other than the lungs (such as the abdomen and
spine); therefore, staging for this tumor should include CT of the abdomen and pelvis with

If indicated, is part of multimodal management in combination with radiation therapy and
surgical management
Intermediate-and high-grade variants
Neoadjuvant or adjuvant radiation therapy
Chemotherapy in select patients
Surgical Management
Well-differentiated liposarcoma
Marginal resection without radiation therapy or chemotherapy
En bloc resection with negative margins can be performed if surgical morbidity is low
because this generally is effective for long-term control.
Intermediate-and high-grade variants
Radiation therapy and wide surgical resection
Outcomes
Well-differentiated liposarcoma
Metastasis extremely rare
Risk of local recurrence is 25% to 50% at 10 years.
Dedifferentiation risk is 2% for extremity lesions and 20% for retroperitoneal lesions.
Intermediate- and high-grade variants
Incidence of pulmonary metastasis increases with grade.
5-year survival rate for nonmetastatic liposarcoma on presentation may range from 50% to
80%, with higher grades portending poorer survival.
Myxoid liposarcomas with more than 5% round cells have a higher likelihood of metastasis
and generally are managed via chemotherapy.
Local recurrence is higher in retroperitoneal lesions.
Rhabdomyosarcoma
Overview
Soft-tissue sarcoma of primitive mesenchyme, primarily occurring in children
Most common soft-tissue sarcoma in children/adolescents (embryonal and alveolar types); 4.5
per million children per year; accounting for one-half of pediatric soft-tissue sarcomas but only
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000564
10/51

3% to 4% of pediatric cancers.
50% occur in individuals aged 0 to 10 years.
Histologic subtypes include embryonal (most common), alveolar, spindle cell, mixed-type,
pleomorphic, and rhabdomyosarcoma with ganglionic differentiation.
Embryonal type occurs in infants/children, peaking at age 0 to 4 years. Affects males more
commonly than females
Alveolar type occurs in adolescents/young adults, with equal incidence from age 0 to 19 years;
no male predilection.
Incidence of pleomorphic variant increases with age into adulthood.
Epidemiology
Embryonal type: age 0 to 15 years, greater incidence in male patients
Alveolar type: age 10 to 25 years, no gender predilection
Pleomorphic type: adults older than 45 years
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Embryonal type: most commonly head and neck
Alveolar type: most common in the deep soft tissues of the extremities, followed by the head
and neck and then the genitourinary tract
Pleomorphic type: most common in the skeletal muscles of the extremities, particularly the
thigh
Etiology
Most cases are sporadic; however, increased risk with some genetic conditions, such as Li-
Fraumeni syndrome and neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1).
In alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (Table 1)
60% t(2:13)(q35;q14) translocation resulting in PAX3-FOX1A fusion protein
20% t(1:13)(p36;q14) translocation resulting in PAX7-FOX1A fusion protein
Classification
Tumor, nodes, and metastasis system denotes size/location of the primary tumor/nodal
involvement/presence versus absence of metastasis.

Grade 1: tumor that can be completely removed surgically
Grade 2: tumor has been removed but with positive margins with or without positive regional
nodal involvement.
Grade 3: tumor with no distant spread that cannot be removed surgically
Grade 4: distant metastasis
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Painless mass most common in extremity
May be dependent on location
Physical Examination
Most lesions occur in the head/neck and genitourinary and retroperitoneal locations.
15% occur in the extremities—forearm, thigh, foot, hand—with incidence equal in the upper
and lower extremities.
Often rapidly enlarging, deep, painless soft-tissue masses
May have lymph node involvement
Staging should include bone marrow biopsy.
Imaging Studies
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Indeterminate: low signal intensity on T1-weighted images; high signal intensity on T2-
weighted images (Figure 5).
Bone Scintigraphy and Positron Emission Tomography
Positron emission tomography (PET) or bone scintigraphy can identify other sites of disease.

Alternating dense hypercellular areas with loose myxoid areas (Figure 6)

Matrix with minimal collagen and more prominent myxoid material

Poor prognostic factors
Histologic subtype matters

Large tumor size
Higher grade
Metastases at presentation
Age older than 35 years
Staging
Given potential lymph node and bone marrow involvement, staging should include
resectability, evaluation of regional lymph nodes (with consideration of sentinel lymph node
biopsy), and bone marrow biopsy.
Management

For nonpleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma, management consists of multimodal chemotherapy
in combination with surgical management and/or radiation therapy.
Common chemotherapy agents include vincristine, dactinomycin, cyclophosphamide, and
ifosfamide.
Surgical resection is preferred for local control. Radiation therapy is indicated for unresectable
lesions, incomplete resection, positive regional lymph nodes, or poor response to
chemotherapy.
Pleomorphic variant is less responsive to chemotherapy; it is managed similar to other soft-
tissue sarcomas.
Outcomes
10-year survival rate by histologic subtype (SEER data)10
Embryonal: 62.9%
Spindle: 49.4%
Mixed: 39.4%
Alveolar: 35.3%
Pleomorphic: 23.1%
For pleomorphic variant in adults, management involves wide resection and radiation therapy.
Chemotherapy is not effective (5-year survival rate of 25%).
Undifferentiated Pleomorphic Sarcoma
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Formerly referred to as malignant fibrous histiocytoma.
No true histiocytic origin was ever demonstrated.
In 2002, the World Health Organization introduced the term UPS because modern techniques
enabled classification of tumors formerly designated as malignant fibrous histiocytoma.
Account for 10% of adult soft-tissue sarcomas
UPS is pleomorphic in histologic appearance.
Epidemiology

16/51

Many are of fibrohistiocytic or fibroblastic lineage.
Also likely include pleomorphic or difficult to identify tumors of other lineages
Demographics
The most common soft-tissue sarcoma in adults aged 55 to 80 years.
Male-to-female ratio is 2:1
More common in Caucasian population than in African American or Asian populations
Related Subtypes
Undifferentiated round cell sarcoma
Undifferentiated spindle cell sarcoma
Undifferentiated epithelioid sarcoma
Etiology
Two etiologic theories
UPS represents many kinds of neoplasms that share morphologic features as they become
progressively more undifferentiated
UPS results from malignant transformation of mesenchymal stem cells (rather than
dedifferentiation of specific lineages).
Genetics
Complex karyotype: no clear causal or diagnostic genetic changes
Cause unknown: can occur in post-irradiation field
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Most are deep seated (subfascial)
History of enlarging mass; may be rapid.
Physical Examination
Mobile mass deep to the fascia in the proximal extremities; lower extremity more common
than upper extremity.
More common in the extremities than the retroperitoneum

Heterogeneous

Storiform or cartwheel growth pattern is observed on low-power histologic images (Figure 9).
Cells are plump, spindled, and arranged around narrow vessels.
Haphazard histiocytic cells
Multinucleate eosinophilic giant cells (Figure 10)

Similar to all high-grade soft-tissue sarcomas, the mainstay of management is wide surgical
excision with adjuvant preoperative or postoperative radiation therapy.1
Outcomes
For high-grade tumors
Metastasis: 30% to 35%, primarily to the lungs
5-year overall survival rate: 65% to 70%
Synovial Sarcoma
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Name originated from the microscopic resemblance of the tumor to mature synovium;
however, the cell of origin is unknown.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Sarcoma Subtypes
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000564
20/51

Distinct lesion occurring in periarticular regions; however, synovial is a misnomer, and it can
occur in any location, including the heart, tonsils, and viscera. It is a distinct lesion frequently
occurring in juxta-articular regions.
Similar to all soft-tissue sarcomas, extremely rare in joint space
Epidemiology
Most common soft-tissue sarcoma in young adults
Most common in individuals aged 15 to 40 years
Affects males more than females
5% to 10% of all soft-tissue sarcomas (800 to 1,000 cases in the United States annually)
Subtypes
Biphasic
Monophasic
Poorly differentiated
Etiology
Genetics/etiology
Characteristic translocation: t(X;18)
Represents the fusion of SYT with either SSX1 or SSX2
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Usually, a painless mass
Time course and size may be variable.
Some may rapidly grow and become large.
Others are slow-growing and remain small, clinically indolent.
In some patients, several years may elapse before a correct diagnosis is made.
Physical Examination

Most common in para-articular regions around the knee, shoulder, arm, elbow, and foot
(lower extremity in 60%)
Can arise from tendon sheath, bursa, fascia, and joint capsule, but only rarely involve a joint
(Figure 11)
Most common sarcoma of the foot
Some have been described as a cause of joint contractures in pediatric patients.
Lymph node examination should be included in the physical examination.
Often slow-growing. In some patients, 2 to 4 years may elapse before a correct diagnosis is
